table.brief: 五列几乎相同类型的短数字（各分店月销量），没有长文本——检验等宽是否自然

understanding.purpose: Compare monthly sales performance across six East China stores for January–May 2024, making store-level trends and month-to-month differences easy to scan.
understanding.reading: Readers anchor on the store name in column 1, then scan horizontally across the five month columns to read a trend; they also compare vertically within a month. Equal month columns are important because those five columns share the same unit and role.
groups: Columns 2–6 (1月–5月) form one measure group: same unit, same role, and should stay equal-width for direct comparison.
Column 1 (门店) is the row-identifier group and should remain visually distinct from the measures.
keep_intact: All four-digit sales values in columns 2–6 must stay on one line without breaking, wrapping, or truncation.
Month headers 1月–5月 and the header 门店 should remain intact.
Store names must remain complete; they may break only between Chinese characters, never lose characters.
may_wrap: Store names in column 1 can wrap to two lines; a three-line fallback is acceptable only if row height permits.
Month headers are too short to need wrapping; numeric cells should never wrap.

preferred.name: r0A
preferred.note: Label-first: give the store column all spare width and hold every month column at the exact minimum needed for four-digit values.

acceptable.name: r0B
acceptable.note: Balanced: use just enough row-label width for two-line store names and share the remaining width evenly across the five month columns.

bad.name: r0C
bad.note: Numeric-first: compress the row label to two-character lines so the month columns become the widest, most open numeric field.
bad.why: Row headers break to three lines, pushing every row to 92px and the table to 593px — 36% taller than needed. The numeric cells then sit in large vertical voids, so the five month columns read as sparse and the eye loses the row rhythm when scanning across; the extra height buys nothing since the numbers were already one line.

bad.name: contrast
bad.note: The tempting 'give the store names room' move: 150px lets every 门店 name sit on one line, but it steals 12px from each month column, leaving 27px of text room where four-digit figures need 39px. Every number then wraps or breaks mid-digit, which is fatal — the reader's whole task is comparing 1284 vs 1197 vs 1452 across a row, and that comparison collapses the moment digits split across lines.
bad.why: The tempting 'give the store names room' move: 150px lets every 门店 name sit on one line, but it steals 12px from each month column, leaving 27px of text room where four-digit figures need 39px. Every number then wraps or breaks mid-digit, which is fatal — the reader's whole task is comparing 1284 vs 1197 vs 1452 across a row, and that comparison collapses the moment digits split across lines.

rationale: Store names are the only unbreakable-ish content that must wrap: 105px of name plus five 39px number columns cannot fit in 391px, so the correct sacrifice is the label column, not the data columns. r0A pushes col 1 to 91px — the maximum the budget allows — so all six names wrap to exactly two lines with balanced breaks, while each month column keeps the 60px it needs to hold four digits on one line. r0B is publishable but spends 3px per month column on empty space (63px for 39px of digits) and pays for it with uglier name breaks such as 上海徐/汇店. Row height should be driven by the label column, not inflated by it; r0C crosses that line.

general: When a table cannot fit on one line, wrap the label column before the numeric columns: numbers lose comparability when they break, names only lose elegance.

Give every column its measured one-line width plus padding first, then hand any surplus to the column with the longest prose content — surplus spread evenly across narrow numeric columns is pure waste.
Row height is set by the tallest cell; keep the tallest cell at two lines and never let a header or label column dictate three, since extra row height is paid on every single row.
Chinese text breaks anywhere, so the label column's width should be chosen so the wrap point lands at a semantically tolerable place and stays consistent across all rows.
specific: Here 105+5×60 = 426 > 391, so ~35px must come out of the label column regardless of design; the only real decision is how to distribute the loss.
Five nearly identical month columns (39/38/39px) should be equal width — they are peers in a time series and any asymmetry would imply a hierarchy that does not exist.
The 门店 column is a row-header, not a data column: it should be as wide as possible (91px) but is the correct place for the wrap.

tradeoffs: Some designers would prefer r0B for its more even column widths (76 vs 63) and would argue that an 11px gap between the label column and the month columns looks more balanced than r0A's 31px drop; others would sacrifice a line of the table by accepting a 3-line label in exchange for a wider name column. Equalising month widths at 65px (r0C) is defensible only if the store names are considered the primary content.
uncertain: Whether two-line wrapped store names are acceptable at all in a publication context, or whether the table should instead be rotated/restructured (e.g. stores as columns) — the width budget is genuinely too tight for the ideal one-line-everything layout, so every design here is a compromise rather than a clean solution.

critique.good: The five month columns are equal at 60px, the true minimum for 39px four-digit values, so all numbers stay intact and directly comparable. The 91px store column is the widest possible under the 391px budget and gives consistent 4+1 or 4+2 store-name breaks. Rows stay compact at 66px and the header/number alignment is clean.
critique.problems: Store names still wrap, and five-character names leave a lone 店 or a short 口店/路店 suffix on the second line. This is visually slightly weak but is forced by the width budget, not by a bad allocation.
critique.cause: Column 1 has 70px of text area, enough for four Chinese characters but not the full 105px one-line store name. The five month columns consume 300px minimum, leaving only 91px for 门店.

critique.good: Month columns are comfortable and the numbers have extra breathing room. No mid-word splits or numeric wrapping occur.
critique.problems: The store column is too narrow: names break 3+2 and split branch names such as 徐汇, 西湖 and 新街口. The rows remain 66px, but the row headers look fragmented. Each month column wastes about 3px that should have gone to column 1.
critique.cause: Column 1 is only 76px, leaving 55px of text, which fits three Chinese characters but not four. The 63px month columns are 3px wider than necessary each, wasting 15px total.

critique.good: Month columns are the roomiest, so numbers never crowd, and the header row stays on one line.
critique.problems: Store names collapse into three short lines, row heights jump to 92px, and the table grows to 593px. Vertical scanning becomes slow, and names lose their semantic grouping. The month columns waste 5px each.
critique.cause: Column 1 is 66px, giving only 45px of text, less than three Chinese characters. The 65px month columns waste 25px total, but that space cannot be recovered without making the table wider than allowed.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r0B.why: Two-line rows stay compact and the month columns comfortably hold every four-digit value, but the 3+2 wrap cuts through store/branch names (上海徐/汇店, 杭州西/湖店), which slows row identification.

r0C.why: The narrow first column preserves natural two-character chunks, but most store names need three lines, making rows tall and the table slower to scan while the month columns carry unused width.

ref_auto.why: The wider first column keeps four-character place/branch names intact and all numbers still fit; the main flaw is the isolated 店 suffix on several second lines, which is awkward but readable.

r0A.why: Same as C: strong preservation of 上海徐汇, 杭州西湖, 苏州观前, etc., with all numeric columns fitting; the lone 店 on the second line is the visible typographic compromise.

ref_equal.why: Like B, it breaks labels into natural two-character chunks but forces three-line rows and leaves the numeric columns wider than necessary, so the table reads tall and the first column feels cramped.

raw.unsure: C and D look identical at this resolution; I may be missing a few pixels of difference. The main judgment call is whether C/D's intact four-character names outweigh the orphaned 店 suffix compared with A's more balanced but semantically disruptive 3+2 breaks.

r0C.why: The row-header column is far too narrow: store names break into three short lines, fragmenting each row and making the table tall and hard to scan. The month columns are wider than their four-digit values need, so width is wasted where it is least useful.

ref_auto.why: A sensible balance: the store column is wide enough for most names to wrap into two lines with the branch name largely intact, while the month columns comfortably hold four-digit values. Rows remain readable as units, though some names still break awkwardly and a lone “店” is orphaned.

ref_equal.why: Essentially the same narrow row-header problem as A: names are chopped into three lines, weakening row identity, while the numeric columns receive surplus width that does not improve legibility.

r0B.why: The wider store column keeps labels to two lines, but the breaks fall mid-branch-name (e.g. 上海徐/汇店, 南京新/街口店), which harms recognition. The month columns are squeezed to the minimum, leaving four-digit numbers with very little breathing room.

r0A.why: Like B, it gives the store column enough room for two-line labels and keeps the month columns comfortable for four-digit values. The table reads row by row more naturally than A/C, despite some unavoidable awkward wraps.

raw.unsure: A/C and B/E appear visually identical or nearly identical, so I cannot reliably distinguish their exact widths; D’s line breaks are also hard to reconcile with its apparently wider first column.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
